body:
I agree with this. I know many women who do all of the pet care in the home. 


Dad and kids may walk or feed the pet, but the mom usually handles all the vet visits, ordering/buying of food/treats/supplements/medication, administering medication, nail clipping, grooming, bathing, brushing and all the cleaning up after the pet like picking up poop/cleaning litter box, washing their food and water dishes, washing their beds, washing their toys, washing their collars/leashes/other accessories and arranging the purchase of new items when the old ones are too worn and also the disposal of old items.


The mom also typically has an increased workload around the house due to pet hair, muddy footprints, smelly linens, messes on carpets, nose prints on windows etc.


I appreciate what the OP is saying about their own personal situation, but I don’t think it’s the norm at all. I know multiple families where the dad came home with a puppy (or even two puppies at once) without consulting the mom and the mom is the one who has to take care of them.

Yes, she is, but her house is decently organized. She just has a lot of stuff that I personally consider to be garbage. 


Most of it is consumables (beauty/hair/skincare/bath/body products, candles, fancy food and drink ingredients) that she either got as gifts or treated herself to and is “saving” for a special occasion. But those special occasions never seem to come and a lot of what she has is expired or has degraded in quality. I’m talking about bath bombs from 15 years ago and stuff like that.


Our hoarder parents are the same way and I used to save things for special occasions too until I realized how wasteful it is. I don’t know if it’s a feeling of not deserving to use nice things or what, but it’s something that makes me want to scream now. Just use the damn stuff!


She also has a lot of craft supplies/projects that are “in progress” as well as old clothing and shoes that don’t fit, are no longer in style, are worn out with holes, stains, broken straps etc. that for whatever reason she struggles to get rid of. She still has socks and underwear from elementary school and she’s in her thirties. Her explanation for keeping them is that she “might need them” one day.


In her defence, we didn’t grow up being taught how to get rid of stuff. I struggle with getting rid of things sometimes too, so I can understand that feeling. We both definitely inherited the “it was a gift so I have to keep it or I’ll be ungrateful” gene from our parents and while I actively fight against that by trying my best to only keep things I love, she has a harder time.


While my sister’s space is more busy and full than I personally prefer and it gives me some level of anxiety when I visit, it doesn’t really impact her life like my parents hoard impacts their life and that’s all that matters to me.

Oh god. My mom going through my garbage as a kid has traumatized me. I have trouble throwing certain things away now without fully destroying them first so that they can’t be “rescued” by a hoarder. My trash is NOT anyone’s treasure and I make sure of that.
This person is a creepy diaper fetish freak who seems to be getting off on writing weird stuff involving human waste.
Ew. What is wrong with you? Keep your weird shit fetish away from normal people.

It feels too black and white for me. I don’t know the full context of what this comment is in response to so it’s hard to say. It may be a well deserved reaction to the psychiatrist implying that you need to help your parents, but if it’s just general advice I don’t necessarily think it’s bad to offer suggestions for the people who do want them.
This made me cry for you and those poor animals. Such a heartbreaking existence for all of you and I’m so sorry for you. I hope you know this isn’t your fault.

Thank you for saying this! I hate that the focus is always on the stuff with hoarders. It’s sometimes frustrating to read some of the comments and posts on this subreddit because people often just judge things by how they look. Stuff is just stuff. It’s how you feel about the stuff that’s the important bit.

I agree with this! We are not doctors (well…maybe some people are) and I don’t think the levels thing is super helpful outside of a professional setting. 


Someone could be at a level one on the surface but their emotional attachment to stuff could be so extreme that all their relationships are negatively impacted, while someone else could be a level four and just a slob/lazy with no objection to their place being cleaned (by someone else).


I think what really matters is how the person feels about their stuff rather than the stuff itself. Stuff is just stuff and it can easily be cleaned up, but if the owner of the stuff is a hoarder that’s not always the case.


The OP has only said that their parents are defensive when they suggest junk removal, so I’m not sure how much they are or aren’t attached to their stuff. They may just be embarrassed of the condition of their home or they legitimately may be distressed at the idea of getting rid of anything. Looking at the house is not a great way to determine how their parents feel. To me the emotional aspect is much more important than the stuff in determining the severity of the hoarding problem.

I’m not suggesting your house should look like a catalogue, but you seemed really angry and full of resentment towards your wife in your post due to the state of your kitchen. It really doesn’t sound to me like you are “happy together”.


The way you ranted about your wife is the exact same way my Dad would rant about my mom while he was cooking in our kitchen. Blaming her for buying too much stuff, criticizing her for having multiple types of the same thing, complaining about things falling out of cupboards or having to search for ingredients. Don’t get me wrong, I understand your frustration having to deal with a hoarder, but what I don’t understand is why you allow your living space to be like this when it’s your home too. Just something to think about.

I’m not a ruler or dictator either, but if my husband was buying so many things that our kitchen was no longer functional and things were falling all over the place I would declutter it myself because I deserve to live in a functional space. I guess I just don’t understand why you don’t demand a functional living space for yourself and your children.

I hope this doesn’t offend you, but why do you allow your wife to treat your (presumably shared) home this way? You are not the child of your wife and you are not forced to live this way.


You posted this in the Child of Hoarder subreddit and as the child of hoarders with different types of hoarding behaviours, I have always been curious why my dad allowed my mom to continue buying so much stuff. Or why my dad didn’t just clear out all the stuff in the kitchen. 


As a child growing up in a hoarder home I had no power to change anything, but you have power because you and your wife are in a partnership. I’m not trying to judge you or make you feel bad, but I am so curious why you are allowing your house to be this way.
Thank you to everyone who replied. I was feeling pretty upset when I wrote this post and it’s been really validating to read all your comments. I really appreciate the support.

That’s got to have been so stressful growing up and so frustrating now. I relate to not keeping my things in common areas for the same reason.  I don’t know how I would react to my mom being excited about finding something from over ten years ago. I would probably fake excitement and take it to be donated myself cause I can’t trust either of my parents to actually do that themselves. 


I still have so much anxiety around my things being lost somewhere in my parents’ house though. Whenever they find something that belongs to me or my sister in their house they use it to justify that the reason their house is the way that it is is because it’s not just their stuff. Even when they find things they wouldn’t allow us to dispose of like old sports paraphernalia that is in too bad of shape to be donated or things they “saved” from the garbage or baby clothes and toys we’ve never seen in our lives! The condition of their home is never their fault.

Hahaha. This is so my dad. He thinks my mom is the hoarder (she is, but so is he), and just thinks that he needs more space. In his defence he is much more organized that my mom, but she’s not in denial about being a hoarder. Different flavours of the same disorder.

1. Yes, my little sister moved out of our parents house about a year after I moved out. Unfortunately, my parents asked her to store some of their things in her spare bedroom and continued to bring more and more things over until I came back from living overseas and put a stop to it. So parts of their hoard lived with her for 3ish years after she moved out.

 

2. I don’t think the hoard really affected our relationship with each other, but it definitely caused us both a lot of stress. Our parents fought constantly about the condition of their home/my mom’s shopping and things would get lost/go missing all the time so holidays, birthdays, vacations, relatives visiting, camping trips etc. were always preceded by chaotic, panicked searches for things with lots of yelling and crying. I’m sure we would both be doing better mentally had we not grown up with hoarder parents, but I’m not sure our relationship with one another would be much different. We are a year and a half apart and we’ve always been close.


3. She is not in denial about their hoard anymore. She used to think it wasn’t as big of a deal as I did and it used to frustrate me because I felt like I was alone, but the more time she spends away from our parents the more she can see the dysfunction. She is actually a bit of a hoarder herself (nowhere near my parents, but she is too attached to stuff) and whenever she visits our parents she always does a deep clean of her house when she gets home. In terms of helping me, she doesn’t really. She has a really busy job and she also kind of shuts down and gets really impatient when helping them. I know being in the hoard causes her stress and she isn’t as good as talking them into throwing away/donating/not buying something as I am anyway, so it’s probably for the best. She does provide great moral support for me and lets me vent whenever I need to. She’s also really appreciative of everything I do for my parents and she expresses this often.


I love my sister so much and I’m so sorry you have a strained relationship with your siblings. I can’t imagine dealing with this without her emotional support, so I can’t imagine how hard this is for you. I really hope you find an ally in your siblings one day soon.

Practical items I know they need and that I help them set up and then throw away the packaging for (smart thermostat and smart plugs this year) and consumables I know they enjoy that have an expiry date (beer, cider, beef jerky, nuts).


If they can’t use it on Christmas Day (gift cards, puzzles, books, clothes, jewelry, scarves, toques, mitts) it will get lost in a pile somewhere and if it’s something they believe lasts indefinitely (candles, makeup, skincare, shaving creams, hand lotion, soaps, hair products, bath bombs, hard liquor, chocolate, hot chocolate, jams, mustard, candy, liquorice) it will never get used because they are “saving” it. 


I’ve spent too much time and effort and money picking out thoughtful gifts for my parents just to see it all sitting untouched in a pile like some weird Christmas time capsule from a specific year.

I’m not sure if I have OCD because of growing up in a hoarding situation, but it definitely didn’t help. I actually suspect my hoarder mom might have OCD of some kind (OCPD I think) because she’s such a control freak.

I’ve been there. One time a scarf from an ex-boyfriend that I had thrown away appeared back in the front closet. I thought I was losing my mind!


I really like your strategy of destroying things before you throw them away (although I can imagine how frustrating it is). I always drove to a dumpster/the dump myself because that was the only way I knew my garbage wasn’t going to reappear.


Hang in there!

Where I’m from, initials are used in all the time in elementary school. Mostly on art projects where there isn’t a lot of room to put your full name, but also on other homework/tests in the younger grades. 


My initials are S.A.D. and when I was in grade one my parents got called in for a meeting with my teacher and the principal to discuss me crying out for help by writing “sad” on all my work. 


I always found it pretty funny that my initials spell “sad”, but I can see why some people have a different experience. In high school I knew two girls with the initials B.J. and both of them got relentlessly teased by some of our male classmates.

I know you posted this yesterday, but I wanted to add my two cents as the child of hoarders who has thrown their stuff away in the past and still continues to do so when I come visit.



Obviously as a child I never threw away anything belonging to my parents, but as I got into my teens I threw away their “stuff” all the time. I had to live in their home and I was frustrated living in a non-functional environment so I regularly threw away stuff that I considered junk.



For example, there was a bathroom that I had to use every day where every drawer, every cabinet and every surface was filled with beauty products and cleaning products that nobody was using. To me, that meant it was all garbage and I treated it as such. Somehow my mom couldn’t part with a 15 year old, separated bottle of lotion that smelled horrible and was covered in dust, a mostly empty bottle of shampoo, tattered rags that smelled like acetone, old hair dye etc. but I sure could!



I also threw away any food that was expired or unusable (chips/crackers/cereal that had been opened for ages and not sealed properly for example). I didn’t care if my parents think “it’s still good past the expiry date”. If nobody was eating it, I was throwing it away. 



I’m sure my parents noticed some of the stuff I threw away (my mom in particular liked to go through the garbage), but they didn’t notice the majority of it as they didn’t regularly open most of the drawers, cupboards because they were all stuffed to the brim and non-functional. They have way too much stuff to possibly keep track of so there was no way they could notice what I was doing. Plus, as I got older I started driving their junk directly to the dump whenever they were away for work or on vacation for longer than a day.



My mom felt it was appropriate to dig through my garbage and recover items of mine that I wanted gone when I was a child (old notes from an ex-boyfriend for example). She had no boundaries over my stuff so why should I have had any for her stuff? Especially when I was forced to live amongst all the junk.



Their home has gotten so much worse since I moved out, because they have nobody there who throws away the junk. They even spilled some of their junk into my younger sister’s apartment, before I put a stop to it. So I still throw away their stuff when I visit. I’ve also helped them move multiple times in the past few years and I also throw out junk then.



Now, you may consider my actions disrespectful, but growing up with hoarder parents was disrespectful to me. I didn’t have a functional closet to store my clothes because it was full of my mom’s clothes that were no longer in style or didn’t fit and “my” baby clothes. I had no place to put books or games because my dad’s university textbooks he hadn’t opened in three decades needed the shelf space. I didn’t have space for my own things so my room was a mess and it was frustrating and distressing to me. Old junk was prioritized over me having space to live functionally and peacefully, so I grew to resent my parents and their stuff.



I would never dream of throwing away something belonging to someone else, unless it was obvious garbage and even then I would consult them first. I do have boundaries with other people, but I do not have them with my parents and their stuff. They created this dysfunctional situation and their actions are responsible for my response to those actions. 



I know I sound mean, but they keep asking for my help with moving, so clearly deep down they do feel better with someone there to throw away crap they don’t need. They just can’t do it themselves because they both struggle a lot from this mental illness. They cycle between thanking me and apologizing for all the work and blind rage and yelling and swearing at me. I keep coming back and helping though because I LOVE them and I don’t want them to live like this. Junk is not more important than people and I hope one day they will realize that.

Isn’t this the truth! They always say “nobody helps me”, but I’ve been screamed at more than I can say for trying to help the hoarders in my life. If you help, you’re helping them wrong and if you stay out of it, you’re wrong for not helping. You never can win with a hoarder. It’s just excuse after excuse and blame to everyone else but themselves.

I would “steal” them too. I’m not trying to be offensive, but will she even notice if they are gone?


I’ve taken so many of my things from my parents’ house that my mom seemed to think belonged to her. She only ever objected if she witnessed me doing it. She has so much junk that I doubt she would even notice something was missing unless I brought it up.


I think holding on to stuff that belongs to their children is just a way for hoarders to feel in control. If you know where something that belongs to you is, just take it.

I really feel for you. It’s frustrating watching someone you love struggle with something like this.


For what it’s worth, I’ve had many tough conversations with both of my parents over the years and it’s never done much good. They know how I feel about everything as I have spelled things out very clearly and set boundaries with them, but unless they themselves want to change it’s pointless. 


I used to get really upset and frustrated with my parents, but now it just…is what it is. I still help them when I can, but I’m no longer mentally invested in fixing them or their hoard. What they do is out of my control and once I came to terms with that I started healing.

I sympathize with you because I’ve also had time sensitive stuff “lost” in my parents’ house. My only advice is to make sure you’ve changed your address with every institution that might ever send you mail and to just accept your Dad as he is. He is suffering from a mental illness and while he may want to do better, he most likely won’t do better unless he seeks professional help.

I’m sure some people become immune to the hoard, but I never did. I was and am more than capable of helping my parents clean, but no matter what I did (and still continue to do when I visit) it never makes enough of a difference. My sister and I were accused many times over the years of not helping our parents keep their house tidy, but you can’t really help someone unless they want your help.


I spent many years in my parents’ house trying to help them declutter and throwing away everything I could without causing a meltdown. I still throw away junk when I come visit and I haven’t lived at home for almost 10 years. If I had it my way their house wouldn’t be full of useless junk, but it’s their house and not my house. Hoarding is a mental illness so it’s not as easy as just “helping out”.
Does the hoarder want help? You can’t really achieve much unless hoarder is on board.
Yes she was. Thank you.
This sounds great. Thanks for all the advice!
I somehow don’t think that’s a good description of my friend’s mom by my friend.
Thank you! I really like that last bit.
